title: ‘I’ll take the rap for that’: labour hire boss asked for fake invoices for sports club sponsorships, Big Build royal commission hears
summary:
Invoices, including for junior football and netball sponsorships totalling thousands of dollars, were part of ‘distorted’ payments to CFMEU official, inquiry told

  • Get our

blocks.text: A labour hire company distorted payments, including to a former top CFMEU official, by creating fake invoices for sports club sponsorships worth thousands of dollars.
BK Labour Hire director Bernard Kearney continued his evidence to the royal commission into alleged corruption across Victoria’s construction sector on Thursday.
The company had an enterprise bargaining agreement with the CFMEU, which helped it get lucrative contracts on Big Build projects beginning around 2022, the commission was told on Wednesday.

The company came under scrutiny from industry regulator the Labour Hire Authority in September 2025 over cash withdrawals totalling $77,970 and transfers to various entities in the name of the former senior CFMEU organiser Joe Myles, totalling $127,472.
Rather than provide a statutory declaration explaining the transactions as requested by the regulator, Kearney admitted to requesting fake invoices be made up.
“I’ll take the rap for that, yep,” he said.

The fake invoices included sponsorships to the Kangaroos Junior football club, Parkdale Vultures football and netball club, Yarra Jets Junior football club, and Port Melbourne bowling club, totalling thousands of dollars.
However, Kearney maintained Myles was paid through his companies for work he had done, describing him as an asset for his knowledge on health and safety procedures.
“Why didn’t you just reply to the Labor Hire Authority and tell them that,” the commissioner, Chris Kourakis, asked.
“Honestly, commissioner, I can’t answer that,” Kearney replied.
The commission heard on Wednesday that BK Labour received a succession of invoices from Myles totalling $256,000 over about a year.
Myles was sacked by the union in mid-2024.
When shown one of the fake invoices with handwriting on it, Kearney initially said it was his, but when told to provide an example of his handwriting on a piece of paper admitted it was not.
Kourakis accused Kearney of a deliberate effort to withhold information from the commission.
“You have just confessed to giving false evidence about writing that note on the invoice,” the commissioner said.

Kourakis suggested Kearney was trying to protect his business partner Duane Allen.
“You’re trying to keep him out of it, aren’t you,” he asked.
“No, no, no,” Kearney replied.
On Wednesday, Kearney was also grilled over $165,000 the company paid to the union-aligned Bandidos gang member Joel Leavitt.
Kearney admitted Leavitt had not provided any work for the firm but said he had “just decided to pay it and move on”.
“I can’t answer why,” he said.

The counsel assisting the commission, Chris Carr, said there were likely only a couple of reasons why BK Labour would have paid Leavitt, including a fear of violence or to suppress some information he had on them.
“Was it one or both of those two?” Carr asked.
“Neither,” Kearney said.
